Nothing here ever holds a credential value — only the NAME of the variable and the PATH of the file that holds it. See README.md for the contract.

connectors.answers: Patent prior art and patent-literature extraction: US and EP publications — bibliography, claims (parsed into independent/dependent tree), full description text, drawings, INPADOC family and legal events, applicant/inventor/title-abstract search.
connectors.why_it_matters_here: SKILL.md source_types names standards and formal literature but had no patent channel at all. Patent specifications are primary sources for method and parameter extraction in applied fields, and OPS carries US publications months before Google Patents indexes them.
connectors.access_ceiling_note: US: full text only when Google Patents has the document; otherwise OPS bibliography + scanned original = [partial]. EP: full text from Google Patents or OPS, in the FILING LANGUAGE only (a DE applicant's EP case is German).

start.human: python run.py  (or double-click run.bat, which also opens a browser)

endpoints.use_for: THE FRONT DOOR. A number returns a card, anything else returns a search list. Use this, not /api/patent.
US numbers only — measured 2026-08-26: rejects 'EP1000000A1' with 'cannot interpret as a US patent number'.
Local corpus inventory (already-fetched patents). Costs no OPS quota — use as the probe and as the reuse-before-re-search check.
What OPS adds for one document. One OPS call, no page bytes.
INPADOC family + legal events. Two OPS calls — only when the question needs family scope or legal status.

secrets.redaction_evidence: src/patentsgrabber/config.py — OpsConfig.describe() and __repr__ return length + last 3 chars only, so a traceback cannot carry the value.

cost.search_trail_label: PatentsGrabber (EPO OPS quota spent: <what the response reported>)

terms.boundary: EPO OPS T&C 3.2 — OPS data itself may NOT be made available to the public (breach -> termination under 8.3). Local reading and quoting into a private deliverable is fine; publishing an OPS-derived dataset or a public page is not.
terms.second_boundary: Google Patents: single-document pages only (robots.txt allows /patent/, disallows search). The tool enforces this; do not work around it.
terms.deliverable_rule: A deliverable built on this connector that the user intends to PUBLISH must have OPS-sourced content flagged so the user can strip it.

connectors.answers: A campus client VPN (a university's or similar) that puts this machine inside an institution's licensed IP range, so subscribed publishers serve full text.
connectors.why_it_is_not_like_anything_else_here: AMBIENT, NOT SCOPED. Every other entry is per-channel: a key affects one connector and nothing else. A VPN changes the network identity of EVERY call this machine makes — WebSearch, WebFetch, citecheck's Crossref and PubMed lookups, PatentsGrabber's OPS calls — all of them become institutionally attributable traffic while it is up. That breaks the premise the whole connector layer rests on (per-connector scope, per-connector consent), which is why it gets its own entry and its own rules rather than being folded into institutional_proxy.
connectors.who_operates_it: THE USER, always. Logging into a client VPN means entering credentials, which the agent must never do. The agent also never ASKS for it to be switched on mid-task: that exports a decision to the user for the agent's convenience, and makes the machine's network identity depend on what the agent happens to be doing.
connectors.assume_off: Never assume it is up, and do not fingerprint the connection to find out. State is known only because the user said so, or because a probe against a specific target reports entitlement. An unstated assumption here silently changes what every other channel is doing.
use_only_when_all_hold: the item is ALREADY IDENTIFIED — a specific DOI or paper the P1 target list named — never exploratory browsing
an extraction target genuinely needs full text that is otherwise [abstract]
the user is actually entitled to it through the institution
it is a small number of documents in this run
never: systematic or bulk downloading — this is the clause institutional licences actually forbid, and the account it costs is the USER's, not the agent's
crawling, or fetching 'while we are in there anyway'
anything that would have worked without it
connectors.window_hygiene: The non-obvious one. While the VPN is up, calls with nothing to do with the entitlement also ride it: resolving 40 DOIs against Crossref appears to Crossref as institutional traffic. Not harmful, but not what the user consented to when they connected for one paper. So do discovery and identifier resolution OUTSIDE the window, and keep the window narrow: connect, fetch the named documents, disconnect.
connectors.volume_gate: More than ~5 documents through it in one run: stop and ask. Not because 6 is dangerous, but because the shape of a run that wants 20 is a bulk download wearing a different name.

secrets.note: No credential the agent can hold. The VPN login is the user's; the agent never sees it and never drives the client.

cost.meter: documents fetched inside the window, counted and reported
cost.search_trail_label: institutional VPN window (N documents; discovery and resolution done outside it)

terms.boundary: Publisher licence terms bind the DELIVERABLE too: content obtained under an institutional licence is for the user's own research use and must not be redistributed. Flag it in anything the user might publish, same as the EPO OPS 3.2 rule.

connectors.blocked_on: Needs a live authenticated session (EZproxy / Shibboleth). A session cookie is a credential AND a personal identity: it must live in a .env-class file behind a fetch script, never in a chat window, and it expires.
connectors.user_action: Decide whether this is acceptable at all. It carries a real risk the other entries do not: bulk automated fetching through an institutional proxy gets accounts suspended. If yes, the safe shape is a fetch-ONE-document CLI with a hard rate cap, not a general proxy.

connectors.answers: Physics/math/CS preprints — discovery, identifier resolution, and the published-version check. The single most useful channel for this user's fields.
connectors.premise_correction: Registered after CORRECTING the premise that prompted it. The user said their email is registered with arXiv, implying that unlocks something. Verified 2026-08-27 against arXiv's own Terms of Use for APIs: the API requires NO account and NO key, and never has. An arXiv account unlocks nothing here.
connectors.what_the_contact_actually_buys: Two real things, neither of which is access. (1) A contact-bearing User-Agent is the politeness convention; arXiv has been returning repeated 429s since ~2026-02-25 even to clients that pace themselves, and an identified client is the one that can be un-blocked rather than guessed at. (2) Identification is the channel for REQUESTING a higher rate, which arXiv's ToU explicitly invites — that request needs a real contact.

invoke.pacing: 1 request per 3 seconds, ONE connection at a time (arXiv ToU, verified 2026-08-27). Never parallelise; never retry-loop a 429 — back off once, retry once, then degrade per the ladder.
invoke.contact_header: User-Agent carries mailto:<user's address> for arxiv.org and export.arxiv.org ONLY — see verify/citecheck.py CONTACT_BY_HOST

secrets.note: No credential. The user's EMAIL is the identifier, and consent for it is per-service: approved for arXiv 2026-08-27, explicitly NOT for Crossref's polite pool or Unpaywall, both declined the same day. A single shared User-Agent would have silently overridden that, which is why the contact is host-scoped in code rather than global.

connectors.known_limits: WebFetch sends its own User-Agent, so the polite contact applies only to this skill's own scripts. Queries made through WebFetch are anonymous to arXiv and carry the ordinary 429 risk.

connectors.answers: Real bibliographic metadata for the SAME files local_pdf_library indexes: DOI, journal, full author list, abstract, dates, pages. The citation fields a filename cannot carry.
connectors.why_it_matters_here: local_pdf_library can say a paper IS in the library but not what its DOI is, so every local hit still cost an identifier-resolution round-trip. Measured 2026-08-27 via `python zotero_local.py --stats`: 157 items, 126 with a DOI (80%), 99 with an abstract, 114 with a PDF on disk. Those hits now start from a real identifier instead of a guess from a filename.

invoke.annotation_tool_authors_note: Author names a pre-annotating tool writes its marks under (user ruling R4, 2026-09-14: an AI-assisted library is expected). Empty until such a tool exists; until declared, its signed marks read as named, never as owner.
invoke.read_pattern: COPY THEN READ. Zotero holds a write lock while running and a reader that hits a mid-write page gets a corrupt answer rather than an error. The tool copies the file and opens the copy read-only, so it works whether or not the app is open — which is also why it does not use the local HTTP API on 127.0.0.1:23119, since that needs the app running.

connectors.access_ceiling_note: [full] only for items with a PDF actually on disk; an item with perfect metadata and no attachment caps at [abstract]. `--stats` prints both counts, and the shortfall belongs in gaps.
connectors.known_limits: NOT a citation authority — the fields are whatever the import put there, so a wrong DOI in Zotero is wrong here too. This removes the LOOKUP, not the VERIFICATION: load-bearing items still go through P2 identifier resolution and the P4.5 support-span check. Items without a DOI (measured 2026-08-27: 31 of 157) still need full resolution, and 43 of 157 have no PDF on disk so they cap at [abstract] however complete the metadata looks.
connectors.relation_to_local_pdf_library: Same files, two views, joined on the Zotero item key (`item_key` in pdf-index.json, `--resolve <KEY>` here). Use pdf_index for fast filename search over what is on disk; use this when the hit needs to become a citation.

cost.search_trail_label: Zotero library (local sqlite, read-only; N of M items carry a DOI)
